accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is strongest (hospitalization rate mapped to H). Complexity increase is modest (adds H) and avoids extra flexibility from delay/fractional terms. Despite identifiability risk for H in a single season (31 train weeks), this is the cleanest target-aligned baseline to test before adding delay or fractional memory.

Still target-aligned via H and adds only a minimal 1-week lag consistent with surveillance semantics. Slightly higher peak-timing sensitivity than no-delay, but remains simpler and more interpretable than fractional+delay. Reasonable to include given explicit note that admissions may lag I.

Uses recommended observation map (delayed_I) and matches the series’ current discovered pattern family (SIR/SEIR with obs=I). For short single-season data where H may be weakly identifiable, delayed_I can be more plausible/robust than adding an H compartment, though it risks amplitude mismatch to hospitalization-rate target.

rejected.reason: Fractional memory is not clearly justified by the provided series summary (single-season, high peakiness but no explicit long-memory evidence). Adding fractional order on top of an already weakly identifiable H compartment increases overfitting/identifiability risk without improving observation-target alignment beyond proposal 0.

Compounded flexibility (fractional + delay + explicit H) is likely over-complex for 31 training points and a single season. High identifiability risk (tradeoffs among delay, fractional order, and H transition rates) and elevated chance of unstable peak timing/width in extrapolation.

suggested_edits.edit: Constrain interpretation to a fixed 1-week observation/reporting lag only (avoid also implicitly allowing additional effective lag via very slow H outflow); keep parameterization as parsimonious as possible to reduce I->H vs H-outflow tradeoffs.

Clarify that delayed_I is being used as an admissions proxy (incidence-like) rather than prevalence; if the template definition allows, ensure the observed quantity corresponds to a lagged flow into I (or a lagged incidence proxy) rather than raw I level, to better match hospitalization-rate semantics without introducing an H compartment.
